title: Colorado business council's 49 fixes face test after Amendment 87
h1: A Colorado business council has 49 ideas to make the state more competitive, and a new income tax and a budget gap stand in the way
description: The Governor's Competitiveness Council roadmap lists 49 recommendations for Colorado. A November 12, 2026 Colorado Sun report weighs them after Amendment 87.
standfirst: Faster permits, simpler sales taxes and reworked incentives top the list. Council members say last week's tax vote makes the job harder, and one economist asks who will pay for it.
keywords: Colorado Competitiveness Roadmap 2026, Governor's Competitiveness Council, Colorado business climate, Amendment 87 businesses, Colorado job growth incentives, Colorado labor force
takeaways: The Colorado Competitiveness Roadmap 2026 lists 49 recommendations in six areas and 19 actions to start this legislative session.
Colorado's labor force peaked at 3.27 million in October 2024 and was down nearly 95,000 as of last month, The Colorado Sun reported.
The state approved its 28th job-growth incentive of 2026 last month, one more than in all of last year.
body: A council of Colorado business leaders wants the state to speed up permits, simplify sales and use taxes and redesign its business incentives. Whether any of that happens is less certain after voters approved a graduated income tax last week, The Colorado Sun reported on Thursday, November 12.

The Governor's Competitiveness Council describes itself as a coalition of business leaders, current and former state officials, economic development groups and educators. Its Colorado Competitiveness Roadmap 2026 lists 49 recommendations in six areas: regulatory reform (7), tax and fiscal policy (9), capital and scale (8), talent and workforce (7), affordability and housing (8), and infrastructure and site readiness (10). It names 19 actions to begin this legislative session.

The report came out in October after listening sessions over the summer, the Sun reported. Ideas include designating "site ready" locations, running permit reviews by several agencies at the same time, and making incentive tax credits refundable and transferable. Some need new money and some need legislation.

Colorado's labor force peaked at 3.27 million in October 2024 and was down nearly 95,000 as of last month, the Sun reported, citing the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The Colorado Chamber of Commerce said last spring that nearly 100 companies had left or picked another state since 2019.

Amendment 87 raises income tax rates on people and businesses earning more than $500,000 a year and lowers them for those earning under $100,000, according to the Sun. Council member Seth Levine, a Boulder venture capitalist, told the Sun the measure poses serious challenges to the council's goal. Broomfield economist Gary Horvath, who is not on the council, questioned how the ideas would be funded with a $1.6 billion gap in next year's budget.

Yes, state officials say. The Economic Development Commission approved its 28th job-growth incentive of the year last month, one more than in all of 2025, and quantum computing company IonQ chose Boulder for a lab where it plans to hire 150 people, the Sun reported. About 70% of the 175 companies awarded incentives since 2021 picked Colorado.
No formal vote is scheduled. Many of the recommendations depend on the Legislature and on the state budget.

sources.title: Colorado was recently dinged for its business climate. Here's how companies want to fix it.
